summary:
On 1 September 2025 the Transitional Legislative Assembly of Burkina Faso passed, unanimously, a law making consensual same-sex relations a criminal offence. The penalty is two to five years' imprisonment plus a fine, and the law took effect immediately. Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala stated that the terms apply to perpetrators of "homosexual or similar practices", and that foreign nationals who violate the law will be deported.

The prohibition is carried by a revised Personal and Family Code approved by the junta's council in July 2024 as part of a junta-led overhaul of marriage and family law. The code entered into force on 1 September 2025. The criminal code now in force bans homosexual acts and the promotion of homosexuality or similar behaviour. Homosexuality had never before been outlawed in Burkina Faso; an equal age of consent introduced in 1996 has been overturned by the 2025 code.

No partner recognition is available. Article 23 of the Constitution defines marriage as the free consent of a man and a woman and does not authorise same-sex marriage, while pre-existing prohibitions on same-sex marriage and same-sex adoption remain in force. The same article bars discrimination in marriage on grounds of race, colour, religion, ethnicity, caste, social origin or wealth — a list that omits sexual orientation and gender identity.

The law was enacted amid a junta crackdown on opposition, media and civil space, and was passed by the unelected 71-member transitional parliament. The military junta has held power since September 2022. France 24–AFP coverage of 22 September 2025 reported fears of a witch hunt and increased self-censorship among LGBTQ people; as of 28 September 2025 no arrests under the law had been reported.

On care access, national adult HIV prevalence stands at 0.80% among those aged 15 to 49. Of an estimated 94,000 adults living with HIV, 65% receive antiretroviral drugs; coverage among children aged 0 to 14 is 28%.
tangentialFactors:
Burkina Faso joins roughly 22 of Africa's 54 states that disallow same-sex relations, placing it within an existing regional pattern of criminalisation rather than an isolated case.

The criminalisation sits inside a wider restriction of civic space under the Traoré junta, which has moved against opposition parties, news outlets and civil society organisations since taking power in September 2022. Reporting from September 2025 describes community-level fear of a witch hunt and rising self-censorship after the law's adoption.

The 2011 Human Rights Report found no legal discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment and occupation, housing, statelessness, access to education or health care, while noting that societal discrimination on those grounds persisted — a gap between formal provisions and lived experience that the new criminal prohibition widens.
localsOnly:
LGBTQ organisations have no legal presence in Burkina Faso but continue to exist unofficially, with no reported violence against them.

Societal discrimination and abuse are documented: LGBT persons have been reported as occasional victims of verbal and physical abuse, religious and traditional beliefs do not accept homosexuality, and there were no reports that the government responded to societal violence and discrimination against them.

Adoption is tightly restricted for residents. Under U.S. Department of State reporting, only married, cohabiting heterosexual couples married for at least five years may adopt, and single applicants are almost never permitted to do so.

HIV treatment coverage among residents has risen substantially, from 32% across all ages in 2010 to 65% of adults living with HIV and 28% of children aged 0 to 14.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources do not state whether the law's prohibition on "homosexual or similar practices" or on promotion reaches gender identity, gender expression or cross-dressing, and no provision on legal gender marker change, identity documents or entry screening is sourced for Burkina Faso.

Unresolved: no data is available on how the promotion offence will be charged, or on prison conditions and treatment of detainees under the new provisions. Enforcement reporting stops at 28 September 2025, when no arrests had been recorded; the position after that date is not sourced here.

The age of consent history (equal at 18 from 1996 until the 2025 code) is documented only as a change of statutory status; the age now set by the revised code is not stated in the sources supplied.
